planting.note: Direct sow in spring (after soil has warmed) into lean, rocky, very well-drained, slightly alkaline soil in full sun; this species comes from canyon and woodland-edge sites in sky island mountain ranges and resents heavy, wet soils far more than it minds heat.

directions: Scarlet hummingbird mint is native to oak-pine canyons and rocky slopes of the sky island ranges of southeastern Arizona, southern New Mexico, and the Trans-Pecos mountains of west Texas (including the Davis Mountains), extending south into the Sierra Madre Occidental of Mexico. It forms an upright, woody-based clump of gray-green, anise-scented foliage topped from midsummer through fall with narrow spikes of vivid scarlet-red to orange-red tubular flowers that are an exceptional hummingbird draw, rivaling any agastache for intensity of bloom color. Give it sharp drainage and lean, rocky soil in full sun; it is markedly less cold-hardy than Agastache cana or A. rupestris and is best treated as a reliably perennial plant only in warmer zones, though it reseeds readily where happy. Avoid rich soil, heavy mulch, and summer overhead watering, all of which encourage crown rot.
sources: Lady Bird Johnson Wildflower Center Native Plant Database

planting.note: Plant seed-sourced or container-grown trees in spring into deep, very well-drained, dry to average, slightly acidic to neutral soil in full sun; this interior variety is adapted to cold winters and summer drought and should not be sited where water stands or soil stays heavy and wet.

directions: Rocky Mountain ponderosa pine is the interior, cold- and drought-adapted botanical variety of ponderosa pine found through the Rocky Mountains, Great Basin, and Colorado Plateau, and in isolated high-elevation sky island ranges of the Trans-Pecos such as the Davis Mountains around Mount Livermore, where it forms open montane woodland alongside Gambel oak and bigtooth maple well above the surrounding desert scrub. Compared to Pacific ponderosa stock, this variety is generally shorter-statured on dry interior sites, has shorter needles typically borne in bundles of two or three, and tolerates colder winters and leaner, rockier soils. The thick, plated, orange-cinnamon bark and open, parklike mature form are shared with the species, and mature bark still carries the characteristic warm vanilla-butterscotch fragrance on hot days. For restoration or landscape plantings in Rocky Mountain, Great Basin, or Trans-Pecos high-desert gardens, seed or stock sourced specifically from this variety establishes and performs far better than generic or Pacific-coast ponderosa seed.
sources: Flora of North America Vol. 2 — Pinus ponderosa var. scopulorum
